# Outliers

## Mental distress and arthritis {.smaller}

Both variables are age-adjusted, model-based county prevalence estimates.

::: question
What observations stand out from the main cloud of points? In what way do they
stand out?
:::


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](16-linear-regression-categorical-outliers_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


## Outliers in regression {.smaller}

::: incremental
- An **outlier** is a point—or group of points—that stands out from the rest of
  the data.

- A **leverage point** is horizontally far from the center of the cloud. It has
  the potential to pull harder on the fitted line.

- An **influential point** actually changes the slope or position of the fitted
  line substantially.
:::

::: {.callout-important .fragment}
These categories can overlap: a point can be an outlier, a leverage point, and
an influential point.
:::

::: aside
Source: [Introduction to Modern Statistics, Section 7.3](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/model-slr.html#sec-outliers-in-regression)
:::

## Three counties to investigate {.smaller}

::: question
How would you classify Caldwell, Wake, and Robeson counties?
:::


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](16-linear-regression-categorical-outliers_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


## Outlier: Caldwell County {.smaller}

::: columns
::: {.column width="62%"}


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](16-linear-regression-categorical-outliers_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


:::
::: {.column width="38%"}

- Caldwell is vertically far from the fitted line.

- Its arthritis prevalence is near the center of the observed values.

- Removing Caldwell barely changes the slope.

::: fragment
**Outlier, but not a leverage or influential point**
:::

:::
:::

## Leverage point: Wake County {.smaller}

::: columns
::: {.column width="62%"}


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](16-linear-regression-categorical-outliers_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


:::
::: {.column width="38%"}

- Wake is horizontally far from the center of the cloud.

- It falls close to the fitted line: its residual is only
  0.21 percentage points.

- Removing Wake barely changes the slope.

::: fragment
**Leverage point, but not an influential point**
:::

:::
:::

## Influential point: Robeson County {.smaller}

::: columns
::: {.column width="62%"}


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](16-linear-regression-categorical-outliers_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


:::
::: {.column width="38%"}

- Robeson is horizontally far from the center of the cloud.

- It also falls far below the fitted relationship: its residual is
  -1.35 percentage points.

- It pulls the right side of the fitted line downward.

::: fragment
**Outlier, leverage point, and influential point**
:::

:::
:::

## With and without Robeson {.smaller}


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](16-linear-regression-categorical-outliers_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


The fitted slope is 0.859 with all counties and
0.893 without Robeson.

## Working with outliers {.smaller}

- Investigate why the observation is unusual:
  - Is it a data or measurement error?
  - Is it a genuine but exceptional case?
  - Does it reveal a subgroup or a missing variable?

. . .

- Fit the model **with and without** the observation and compare the results.

. . .

- Do not remove an outlier solely because it is unusual. Report and justify any
  decision to exclude data.

::: aside
Source: [Introduction to Modern Statistics, Section 7.3](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/model-slr.html#sec-outliers-in-regression)
:::



# Categorical predictor

## A new question

::: question
How does estimated frequent mental-distress prevalence vary by county
development tier?

How are the variables in this analysis different from those in our model from
last time?
:::

. . .

-   outcome: frequent mental-distress prevalence (numerical)

-   predictor: county development tier (categorical; Tier 1 is most
    economically distressed and Tier 3 is least economically distressed)

## Visualize mental distress vs. development tier {.smaller}

::: question
Determine whether each of the following plot types would be an appropriate
choice for visualizing the relationship between mental-distress prevalence and
development tier.
:::

-   Scatterplot [❌]{.fragment}

-   Box plot [✅]{.fragment}

-   Violin plot [✅]{.fragment}

-   Density plot [✅]{.fragment}

-   Bar plot [❌]{.fragment}

-   Stacked bar plot [❌]{.fragment}

## Boxplot {.smaller}

::: question
Visualize the relationship between mental-distress prevalence and development
tier. Also calculate the average mental-distress prevalence per tier.
:::


::: {.cell output-location='column'}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(
  nc_places,
  aes(x = development_tier, y = mental_distress)
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_label()) +
  labs(
    x = "Development tier",
    y = "Adults experiencing frequent mental distress (%)",
    title = "Mental distress by county development tier"
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](16-linear-regression-categorical-outliers_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::



::: {.cell output-location='column'}

```{.r .cell-code}
nc_places |>
  group_by(development_tier) |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    mean_mental_distress = mean(mental_distress)
  )
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  development_tier     n mean_mental_distress
  <fct>            <int>                <dbl>
1 Tier 1              40                 19.4
2 Tier 2              40                 18.4
3 Tier 3              20                 16.8
```


:::
:::


## Violin plot {.smaller}


::: {.cell output-location='column'}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(
  nc_places,
  aes(x = development_tier, y = mental_distress)
) +
  geom_violin() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_label()) +
  labs(
    x = "Development tier",
    y = "Adults experiencing frequent mental distress (%)",
    title = "Mental distress by county development tier"
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](16-linear-regression-categorical-outliers_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


## Density plot {.smaller}


::: {.cell output-location='column'}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(
  nc_places,
  aes(
    x = mental_distress,
    color = development_tier,
    fill = development_tier
  )
) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_label()) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.85) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(end = 0.85) +
  labs(
    x = "Adults experiencing frequent mental distress (%)",
    y = "Density",
    color = "Development tier",
```

## Multiple geoms {.smaller}


::: {.cell output-location='column'}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(
  nc_places,
  aes(x = development_tier, y = mental_distress)
) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0, size = 2, alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_label()) +
  labs(
    x = "Development tier",
    y = "Adults experiencing frequent mental distress (%)",
    title = "Mental distress by county development tier"
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](16-linear-regression-categorical-outliers_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


## Model - fit {.smaller}

::: question
Fit a linear regression model predicting mental-distress prevalence from
development tier and display the results.

Why is Tier 1 not in the output?
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mental_distress_tier_fit <- linear_reg() |>
  fit(mental_distress ~ development_tier, data = nc_places)

tidy(mental_distress_tier_fit)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 5
  term                   estimate std.error statistic   p.value
  <chr>                     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)               19.4      0.136    143.   1.06e-114
2 development_tierTier 2    -1        0.192     -5.22 1.04e-  6
3 development_tierTier 3    -2.57     0.235    -11.0  1.18e- 18
```


:::
:::


## Model - interpret {.smaller}

$$
\widehat{\text{mental distress \%}} = 19.42 - 1.00 \times \text{Tier 2} - 2.57 \times \text{Tier 3}
$$

-   Intercept: [The predicted average mental-distress prevalence among Tier 1 counties is 19.42%.]{.fragment}

-   Slope — Tier 2: [Tier 2 counties are expected to have, on average, a mental-distress prevalence 1.00 percentage point lower than Tier 1 counties.]{.fragment}

-   Slope — Tier 3: [Tier 3 counties are expected to have, on average, a mental-distress prevalence 2.57 percentage points lower than Tier 1 counties.]{.fragment}

## Model - predict {.smaller}

::: question
What is the predicted mental-distress prevalence for a Tier 1 county?
What are the predicted values for Tier 2 and Tier 3 counties?
Where have we seen these values before?
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
new_counties <- tibble(
  development_tier = factor(
    c("Tier 1", "Tier 2", "Tier 3"),
    levels = levels(nc_places$development_tier)
  )
)

augment(mental_distress_tier_fit, new_data = new_counties)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  .pred development_tier
  <dbl> <fct>           
1  19.4 Tier 1          
2  18.4 Tier 2          
3  16.8 Tier 3          
```


:::
:::


## Model - predict {.smaller}

::: task
Calculate the predicted mental-distress prevalence for counties in each
development tier *by hand*.
:::

$$
\widehat{\text{mental distress \%}} = 19.42 - 1.00 \times \text{Tier 2} - 2.57 \times \text{Tier 3}
$$

. . .

-   Tier 1: $\widehat{\text{mental distress \%}} = 19.42 - 1.00 \times 0 - 2.57 \times 0 = 19.42$

. . .

-   Tier 2: $\widehat{\text{mental distress \%}} = 19.42 - 1.00 \times 1 - 2.57 \times 0 = 18.42$

. . .

-   Tier 3: $\widehat{\text{mental distress \%}} = 19.42 - 1.00 \times 0 - 2.57 \times 1 = 16.85$

## Models with categorical predictors

::: incremental
-   A categorical predictor is encoded using **dummy variables**.
    A predictor with $k$ levels requires $k - 1$ dummy variables.

-   The first level of the categorical variable is the **baseline level**.
    In a model with one categorical predictor, the intercept is the predicted
    value of the outcome for the baseline level (when all dummy variables equal 0).

-   Each slope coefficient describes the difference between the predicted value of the outcome for that level of the categorical variable compared to the baseline level.
:::

## Changing the baseline level

-   By default, R uses the first level of a categorical variable as the baseline level.

-   We can change the baseline level by reordering the levels of the categorical variable.

## Participate 📱💻 {.xsmall}

:::::: columns

:::: {.column width="70%"}

::: wooclap

What function goes in the blank to make Tier 3 the baseline level in the
`development_tier` variable?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
nc_places |>
  mutate(
    development_tier = ___(development_tier, "Tier 3")
  )
```
:::


::: wooclap-choices
- `level_reorder`
- `fct_relevel`
- `fct_reorder`
- `str_relevel`

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
